growth_story.headline: Greenland's fish-based economy grew fast from 1998 to 2008, then slowed to 1.1 percent a year, yet income per person reached a new high in 2023.
growth_story.arc: Greenland's income per person fell by 12.2 percent in 1990, and the era from 1990 to 1997 averaged -1.3 percent a year. From 1998 to 2008 growth picked up to 4.2 percent a year, and income per person passed its 1989 level in 2000. Since 2009 growth has slowed to 1.1 percent a year, close to the 1.4 percent average of the last decade, but income per person still reached a new high in 2023. The sources tie the swings to fish: fish products make up most exports, so good catches and high prices bring growth, while poor catches and falling shrimp and cod prices bring slowdowns. A yearly block grant from Denmark helps keep large public administrations, and since self-government came into force in 2009 Greenland has controlled its mineral resources, though fishing, construction and trade remain the main industries.

threads.title: Fish at the core
threads.text: Fishing, construction and trade are the main industries, and fishing and related industries bring in a large share of business revenue. In 2011 the OECD found that fish products made up most of Greenland's exports.

threads.title: Fish cycles and falling prices
threads.text: Swings in the fish industry drive swings in the whole economy: good catches and high export prices have brought growth, and poor catches and weak markets have brought slowdowns. After the global economic crisis, cod and shrimp prices fell, which the OECD called a particular challenge for Greenland because shrimp is its most important catch.

threads.text: A yearly block grant from Denmark supports large sectors that serve the home market, and in 2009 it made up most of government revenue. Outside fishing, jobs grew most after 2000 in trade and construction, which serve the home market rather than exports.

growth_story.tension: In 2011 the OECD wrote that Greenland's income per person had fallen further behind the other North Atlantic territories since 2002 because of slower growth. The data do not show slow growth in those years: after a fall of 1.3 percent in 2002, income per person grew in every year from 2003 to 2008, by as much as 6.6 percent in 2004 and 2008, and the 1998 to 2008 era averaged 4.2 percent a year.
